intro: Underfloor heating is becoming an increasingly popular choice for homeowners in Borthwickrig, and it's easy to understand why. When you're dealing with Scottish winters and properties that can be drafty by nature, the idea of warm floors radiating heat evenly through every room is genuinely appealing. Whether you're renovating a period cottage or finishing out a newer build on one of the modern estates, underfloor heating transforms how a home feels to live in. In a small, close-knit community like Borthwickrig, it's also the kind of investment that adds real long-term value — both in comfort and in what your property is worth on the market.
localContext: Borthwickrig sits in Midlothian's rolling countryside, and the housing stock here reflects that rural character well. Older stone-built properties dominate much of the area, and while they have tremendous charm and solid construction, their thick walls and original flooring can make them less thermally efficient than modern homes. Period cottages in particular often rely on ageing radiator systems that struggle to heat large open rooms evenly. This is where underfloor heating makes a lot of sense — it works with lower flow temperatures, which suits modern heat pumps and condensing boilers alike. It's also worth noting that Borthwickrig sits in a moderately hard water area, which means your pipework and heating system can be more prone to scale build-up over time. Any underfloor heating installation here should include appropriate inhibitor treatment and ideally a magnetic filter to protect the system from limescale and debris. Modern estates in the area tend to be easier to retrofit, but older homes aren't out of the running — they just need careful planning and the right system type.
serviceDetail:
A proper underfloor heating installation in Borthwickrig follows a clear process, and understanding each stage helps you plan the project confidently. It starts with a site survey, where an engineer assesses the property — floor construction, room sizes, existing heat source, and insulation levels. This is especially important in older stone-built properties where subfloor conditions vary considerably. From there, you'll receive a heat loss calculation to determine the correct output needed for each zone, and a system design tailored to your home.

For wet underfloor heating — the most common choice for whole-home installations — pipework is laid in loops across the floor, either into a screed or within low-profile overlay panels that sit on top of existing floors. The screed method is more involved, requiring the floor to be built up and allowed to cure properly before any flooring is laid on top. Overlay systems are quicker and better suited to retrofits in Borthwickrig's older homes where raising floor heights significantly isn't practical.

Once the pipework is in place, it connects to a manifold — essentially the control hub of the system — which links back to your boiler or heat pump. Each room or zone gets its own thermostat for independent temperature control. The system is then pressure-tested, filled, bled, and commissioned. In a moderately hard water area like Borthwickrig, the engineer should also dose the system with corrosion inhibitor at this stage. From survey to commissioning, a full installation typically takes between three and seven days depending on the size of the property.
pricing: Underfloor heating installation costs in Borthwickrig typically fall in the range of £3,000 to £8,000 for a full home installation, though the actual figure depends on several factors. The type of system matters — wet screed systems cost more than electric mat systems or overlay options. Property size is the biggest driver: a three-bedroom cottage will cost considerably less than a larger detached home. Older stone-built properties sometimes require additional groundwork or insulation upgrades before the system can be installed efficiently, which adds to the total. Connecting to a new heat pump rather than an existing boiler also increases the overall project cost. Single-room installations can start from around £800 to £1,500 for electric systems.

faqs.q: Is underfloor heating suitable for the older stone-built properties common in Borthwickrig?
faqs.a: Yes, but it requires careful planning. Stone-built homes often have solid or suspended timber floors, both of which can accommodate underfloor heating with the right system choice. Overlay systems work well for retrofits, avoiding the need for deep screeds. A proper heat loss survey will confirm whether your home's insulation levels are sufficient to make the system efficient.

faqs.q: How does Borthwickrig's moderately hard water affect an underfloor heating system?
faqs.a: Moderately hard water increases the risk of limescale forming inside the pipework and manifold over time, which can reduce efficiency and lead to premature wear. To protect your system, your installer should treat the water with a quality corrosion inhibitor and fit a magnetic filter. Annual servicing that includes checking inhibitor levels will keep the system running well for years.

faqs.q: Can I add underfloor heating to just one room rather than the whole house?
faqs.a: Absolutely. Single-room installations are common in Borthwickrig, particularly in kitchens, bathrooms, and extensions. If you're extending a wet system, your installer will assess whether your existing boiler can handle the additional load.

faqs.q: How long does underfloor heating take to heat up compared to standard radiators?
faqs.a: Wet underfloor heating has a slower response time than radiators — typically one to two hours to reach full temperature — so it's best managed with a programmable thermostat set to warm the home ahead of when you need it. Once up to temperature, it holds heat well and runs efficiently at lower flow temperatures, which suits the condensing boilers and heat pumps increasingly common in Borthwickrig homes.
